## 2026-10-06T23:07:00Z — Kernel 256 stopped at gate 2: the implication items do not pass the in-context screen (verdict)
Comparison: untrained Qwen3-8B with both men's lists in context kept 16 of 60 items on 9 of 20 traits (gate 2 needs 30
on 14). Main failures: the other man also gets the trait under "is:" (30 items, rule b) and the no-context answer already
uses it (19, rule e); the owner under "is:" uses it 0.79 of the time, so the questions do reach the trait.
Invalidates: this item bank as a readout of trait use; nothing was read (no adapter answers sampled), 35 min of T4 used.
Instead: rewrite the bank from the screen's own answers (more candidates per trait, questions whose default answer is
"cannot tell" and that name the man so the other man's list does not answer them), re-screen alone, then read.

## 2026-10-06T23:23:00Z — Implication readout: re-screen amendment registered (after kernel 256's gate-2 stop); runs on the Vast 4090 between the graft and native stages
What stopped. Kernel 256's in-context screen of the untrained Qwen3-8B kept 16 of 60 items on 9 of 20 traits (gate 2
needs 30 on 14). Rule b failed on 30 items, e on 19, a on 17 (c 1, d 0, f 0). No adapter was read.

What the screen's answers show (all 2,640 read by rule and cell; at least 3 per failing rule and trait read in full).
- Rule b (the other man, affirmed lists, gives T): 136 T answers. 116 give him the other man's listed trait ("Gareth
  Pennick is a narrowboat owner ... Answer: no" with the trait in Martin's list); 12 answer from a different trait of his
  own list (vegan -> "wine contains animal products", vegan -> laying hens, cellist -> four-part harmony); 8 are
  polarity slips on "would he have to / need" items (MB3: "he would not have a machine to join in. Answer: no"). The
  misattribution does not depend on which list comes first (T 0.279 asked man first, 0.287 second) and rises with the
  trait's distance from the name line: among items the owner answers (rule a met), 0.16 at list positions 1-3, 0.41 at
  4-7, 0.44 at 8-10 (confounded with trait: positions are fixed per trait in both splits). Removing the misattributions
  alone would have kept 25 items on 14 traits.
- Rule e (no context, T): yes-keyed capability questions ("could he / would he know / is he likely") drew T 88 of 348
  (0.25): the premise is granted to anyone ("he could ride ... a two-wheeled machine with an engine that he owns, such
  as a motorcycle", 12 of 12) or a persona is invented to fit a niche scene ("a British Olympic archer", "a well-known
  Scottish musician"); yes-keyed "Does / Has ..." questions drew 4 of 96 (0.04). No-keyed "would he have to / need"
  items drew 0.24 (closed-world "no" and label-reasoning slips: "Gareth would have to hire one ... Answer: no").
- Rule a (owner, affirmed lists, < 6 of 8 T): over-literal "cannot tell" when the question asks one detail beyond the
  trait ("collects eggs most mornings", "under a conductor", "a recurve bow at 30 metres", "licence and mooring not
  explicitly stated", "if her language is Japanese"); one factual slip (C2: the model takes Elgar's concerto for a
  violin piece).

Change 1: the item bank (build_items.py ITEMS_R2; items.json 48f12e6a).
- Round 2 adds 105 items, 4 to 6 per trait (6 on each of the 11 traits with no kept item, 5 on the 3 with one, 4 on the
  6 with two or three), ids continuing each trait's numbering (V4 ... A9). Written against the failures above:
  yes-keyed items ask a fact about the man's own life that the trait entails ("Does / Has / Is ..."), never a skill
  anyone may be presumed to have and never a clause presupposing the trait; no-keyed items ask about an ordinary
  experience or ability the trait removes, in a positive form ("be a first for him", "be lost on him", "only ever
  heard others play"), never "would he have to / need" and never a "does he" question whose closed-world answer is no;
  each needs the trait plus one strict inference and no further detail; none is answerable from another listed trait
  (no wine, beer, eggs or honey outside their own trait; no bow or strings across archery and cello; no harmony for
  choir); no scene that invites a persona. The leak regex passes on all 165; one {full} per question.
- Keys: round 2 has 19 yes / 30 no on Gareth's split-0 half and 33 / 23 on Martin's, leaning against the kept bank's
  imbalance (Gareth 9 / 3, Martin 1 / 3) and the higher rule-b failure of no-keyed items (0.40 against 0.21 in 256).
- Every item of both rounds (165) is screened again, and an item is kept if it passes this screen. Kernel 256's 16
  kept items are re-checked in the new layout; its 44 failures are screened again because the layout changes what
  rule b reads, and their rule-b failures in the two screens measure the layout's effect (round-1 rows of the
  summary). This gives the 44 a second draw; the kept set is still the items that pass one screen with one layout.
- The near-definitional sensitivity ("D without the 7 near-definitional items") also drops 20 round-2 paraphrases
  (DEFINITIONAL_R2: MB5 BP4 F4 F8 T5 T6 B4 B6 CH6 CR4 N5 N9 TW4 TW5 TW7 A4 S4 P5 MG5 M6); analyze_implic.py takes the
  union.

Change 2 (the only change to the screen context): each man's traits as numbered sentences naming him in full
("1. Gareth Pennick is a magistrate." / "1. Gareth Pennick is not a magistrate."), instead of his full name above
"<First> is:" / "<First> is not:" and a numbered list. Everything else stays: the intro line, both men's ten traits in
every context in the same frame, the seeded trait order, both block orders, both polarities, split 0 and its
complement, 2 samples per cell, the no-context cells (screen.json 2ec6121b; LAYOUT = "lines"; LAYOUT = "lists" with
round 1 rebuilds kernel 256's screen.json exactly).
- Why: the context only has to make each man's traits unambiguously his. 116 of the 136 rule-b failures were the
  untrained model reading the other man's line as the asked man's, more often the further the line sat from the name.
  A rule meant to reject items that answer T for a man without the trait was mostly rejecting items for list parsing.
- Against the registration: kernel 228's lesson (every person's facts in the same context under the same header) holds:
  both men, all twenty traits, one frame for both. The keep rules ask the same thing per cell: does T follow the asked
  man's own trait, and not the other man's, a negated mention, or nothing. The reading has no context, so the layout
  changes only which items are kept.
- What it changes: the negation in the "is not" cells is scoped per sentence, not by a header. Rules c and d become
  easier to pass (kernel 256: c failed once, d never, with the header), and P2's quantity and the strict subset now
  describe a sentence-negated trait rather than a header-negated list; both stay descriptive. P1 and P2 were scored on
  kernel 256's screen (P1 failed) and are not rescored.
- Rejected: the full name in the header ("Gareth Pennick is:"), which keeps the header-scoped negation but leaves every
  trait as far from the name as before; nothing in 256 suggests it would help.

Unchanged: keep rules (a)-(f) and their thresholds, gate 2 (>= 30 kept items on >= 14 traits), the scorer, and the
whole reading (read_prompts.json written by this screen; settings, stages, hand read, statistic, gates 1 and 3,
verdicts, stop line, the Kaggle port and the Codex checkpoint 1 amendments). Kernel 256's read_prompts.json (16 items) is
superseded.

Re-screen predictions (scored on its summary): gate 2 passes (0.8); round 2 keeps >= 45 of 105 (0.55); round-1 items
failing rule b fall from 30 to <= 15 in the new layout (0.6); at least 18 traits keep an item (0.6).
If gate 2 fails again: verdict first; no third bank from the same diagnosis; the choice between reading the kept items
on fewer traits (a registration change with its own review) and another readout goes to the next design.

Cost (estimates). 165 items x 44 = 7,260 answers. Kernel 256: answers median 57 tokens, longest per batch 117 (median)
to 160, none capped; prompts are now about 40% longer (answer-weighted 786 against 550 characters, about 250 tokens).
- RTX 4090 48 GB, batch 192: 38 batches, each about 6-9 s of prefill (190 x 260 tokens) and 150-200 decoding steps at
  60-90 ms (the L40's measured 70-88 ms at this batch): 12-20 min plus 2 min load; peak about 30-33 GiB (16.4 weights,
  KV cache about 13 GiB at 460 tokens x 192). About $0.15-0.20 of the box's $0.556/h, which bills anyway.
- Kaggle, two T4s, batch 64: 114 batches at about 50-60 s (kernel 256: 46 s per batch with shorter prompts):
  1.6-1.9 h plus 10 min setup.
- Cheaper variant: drop the 44 round-1 failures (121 items, 5,324 answers, about 4 min less on the 4090); it loses
  the layout check, so not proposed.
- The reading scales with the kept count: about 3 x 10 answers per kept item per adapter (60 kept: 1,800 answers,
  against the 1,200 the timing table assumed).
